items.readable_text:
Content:
When we have an exponential function in an inequality and the base of the exponential is less than [MATH: 1,] we can't take a logarithm of both sides using that same base. To see why not, consider the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2} \lt 1]

Content:
If we take a logarithm with base [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] of both sides, then we get a false statement:

Content:
[MATH: \log_{(1)/(2)} ((1)/(2))|≮\log_{(1)/(2)} (1); 1|≮0]

Content:
However, we can get around this problem by always taking a logarithm with a base that's greater than [MATH: 1,] such as the natural logarithm [MATH: \ln,] which has base [MATH: e \approx 2.71 \, .] Then we can use the laws of logarithms to simplify the result.

Content:
For example, consider the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^x < 5]

Content:
We can't take [MATH: \log_\frac{2}{3}] of both sides, but we can take the natural logarithm of both sides and simplify the result using the laws of logarithms:

Content:
[MATH: \ln [((2)/(3))^{x}]|< \ln 5; x\ln ((2)/(3))|< \ln 5; x(\ln 2 − \ln 3)|< \ln 5]

Content:
Lastly, note that [MATH: \ln 2 - \ln 3] is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

Content:
[MATH: x|> (\ln 5)/(\ln 2 − \ln 3)]

a. [MATH: x > (\ln 5 − \ln 2)/(\ln 3 + \ln 5)]
b. [MATH: x < (\ln 2 + \ln 5)/(\ln 3 + \ln 5)]
c. [MATH: x > (\ln 5 − \ln 2)/(\ln 5 − \ln 3)]
d. [MATH: x < (\ln 5 − \ln 2)/(\ln 5 − \ln 3)]
e. [MATH: x < (\ln 5 − \ln 2)/(\ln 3 + \ln 5)]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When we have an exponential function in an inequality and the base of the exponential is greater than [MATH: 1,] we can take the logarithm of both sides of the inequality.

Content:
For example, to solve the inequality

Content:
[MATH: 2^x < 3,]

Content:
we can take the logarithm (base [MATH: 2]) of both sides and get

Content:
[MATH: \log_{2} (2^{x})|< \log_{2} (3); x|< \log_{2} (3).]

Content:
The reason why we're allowed to take a logarithm of both sides of an inequality is that taking a logarithm preserves the order of numbers. That is to say, if [MATH: a < b,] then [MATH: \log_n (a) < \log_n (b),] provided that [MATH: n > 1] and [MATH: a,b>0.]

Content:
To see this concretely, consider the following order of numbers:

Content:
[MATH: 0.5 < 1 < 2 < 3]

Content:
If we take the logarithm (base [MATH: 2]) of all the numbers above, they stay in the same order:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{-1}_{ \log_2(0.5) } < \underbrace{0}_{ \log_2(1) } < \underbrace{1}_{ \log_2(2) } < \underbrace{ \,\, 1.585 \,\, }_{ \log_2(3) }]

---

Item 2 — Example: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Greater Than One

Example Prompt:
Solve the inequality [MATH: 4e^x - 5 > 0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

[MATH: 4e^{x} − 5|> 0; 4e^{x}|> 5; e^{x}|> (5)/(4).]

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

[MATH: \ln (e^{x})|> \ln ((5)/(4)); x|> \ln 5 − \ln 4.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Case When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

Content:
When we have an exponential function in an inequality and the base of the exponential is less than [MATH: 1,] we can't take a logarithm of both sides using that same base. To see why not, consider the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2} \lt 1]

Content:
If we take a logarithm with base [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] of both sides, then we get a false statement:

Content:
[MATH: \log_{(1)/(2)} ((1)/(2))|≮\log_{(1)/(2)} (1); 1|≮0]

Content:
However, we can get around this problem by always taking a logarithm with a base that's greater than [MATH: 1,] such as the natural logarithm [MATH: \ln,] which has base [MATH: e \approx 2.71 \, .] Then we can use the laws of logarithms to simplify the result.

Content:
For example, consider the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: \left( \dfrac{2}{3} \right)^x < 5]

Content:
We can't take [MATH: \log_\frac{2}{3}] of both sides, but we can take the natural logarithm of both sides and simplify the result using the laws of logarithms:

Content:
[MATH: \ln [((2)/(3))^{x}]|< \ln 5; x\ln ((2)/(3))|< \ln 5; x(\ln 2 − \ln 3)|< \ln 5]

Content:
Lastly, note that [MATH: \ln 2 - \ln 3] is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

Content:
[MATH: x|> (\ln 5)/(\ln 2 − \ln 3)]

---

Item 6 — Example: Solving an Inequality When the Base of the Exponential is Between Zero and One

Example Prompt:
Solve the inequality [MATH: 5 \cdot \left( \dfrac{3}{4} \right)^x + 2 \geq 12.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

[MATH: 5 ⋅ ((3)/(4))^{x} + 2|≥ 12; 5 ⋅ ((3)/(4))^{x}|≥ 10; ((3)/(4))^{x}|≥ 2.]

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

[MATH: \ln [((3)/(4))^{x}]|≥ \ln 2; x\ln ((3)/(4))|≥ \ln 2; x(\ln 3 − \ln 4)|≥ \ln 2.]

Lastly, note that [MATH: \ln 3 - \ln 4] is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

[MATH: x|≤ (\ln 2)/(\ln 3 − \ln 4)]

Item 9 — Tutorial: Comparing an Exponential to Zero or a Negative Number

Content:
Sometimes we might not be able to find the logarithm of both sides of inequality due to a negative number. For example, this happens in the following inequality:

Content:
[MATH: 3^{x-1} \geq -5]

Content:
We can't take the logarithm of both sides because [MATH: \ln (-5)] is not a real number. In general, a logarithm of a negative number is not a real number.

Content:
What we can do instead, though, is realize that a power of a positive number is always greater than [MATH: 0.] In particular, in our situation, we have

Content:
[MATH: 3^{x-1} > 0]

Content:
for all values of [MATH: x] because any power of [MATH: 3] is positive.

Content:
So, because [MATH: 3^{x-1} > 0] for all values of [MATH: x,] we have [MATH: 3^{x-1} \geq -5] for all values of [MATH: x,] and we conclude that the solution consists of all real numbers.

Content:
Note: If the inequality were flipped, i.e., [MATH: 3^{x-1} \leq -5,] then the inequality would have no real solution. The reasoning is the same: because any power of [MATH: 3] is positive, we must have [MATH: 3^{x-1} > 0] for all values of [MATH: x,] so we can never have [MATH: 3^{x-1} \leq -5.]

Content:
In general, if we have an inequality that compares a power of a positive number to zero or a negative number, it will always be the case that either the solution consists of all real numbers, or there is no real solution.

---

Item 10 — Example: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number

Example Prompt:
Solve the inequality [MATH: 4 \cdot 3^{8-x} + 12 > 0.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

[MATH: 4 ⋅ 3^{8 − x} + 12|> 0; 4 ⋅ 3^{8 − x}|> − 12; 3^{8 − x}|> − 3.]

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than [MATH: 0,] we must have

[MATH: 3^{8-x} > 0]

for all values of [MATH: x.]

Therefore, the inequality [MATH: 3^{8-x} > -3] is satisfied for all real values of [MATH: x.]

Item 13 — Tutorial: Equations with Exponential Functions on Both Sides

Content:
When an inequality has exponential functions on both sides, we can often solve it by taking a logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms.

Content:
For example, consider the inequality

Content:
[MATH: 2^{x} < 3^{1-x}.]

Content:
Taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we solve the equation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \ln (2^{x})|< \ln (3^{1 − x}); x\ln 2|< (1 − x)\ln 3; x\ln 2|< \ln 3 − x\ln 3; x\ln 2 + x\ln 3|< \ln 3; x(\ln 2 + \ln 3)|< \ln 3; x|< (\ln 3)/(\ln 2 + \ln 3)]

Content:
Note: Other times, it's possible to run into cases where there is no real solution, or where the solution is all real numbers. For example, consider the following equation:
[MATH: 2^{x} < -3^{1-x}]

Content:
Since [MATH: 2^x] is always positive and [MATH: -3^{1-x}] is always negative, we always have [MATH: 2^x > -3^{1-x}.] This means the above inequality has no real solutions.

---

[MATH: 3 ⋅ 5^{x}|< 7^{3 − x}; \ln (3 ⋅ 5^{x})|< \ln (7^{3 − x}); \ln 3 + \ln (5^{x})|< \ln (7^{3 − x}); \ln 3 + x\ln 5|< (3 − x)\ln 7; \ln 3 + x\ln 5|< 3\ln 7 − x\ln 7; x\ln 5 + x\ln 7|< 3\ln 7 − \ln 3; x(\ln 5 + \ln 7)|< 3\ln 7 − \ln 3; x|< (3\ln 7 − \ln 3)/(\ln 5 + \ln 7)]
